rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer here is compared with one given through Jesus in 5:115–118.
rows.anchor: given through the tongue of Jesus (sws) in verses 115-118 of S ū rah al-Mā’idah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement about God providing for them and their forefathers until they forgot the reminder parallels 57:16, where prolonged enjoyment hardens hearts.
rows.anchor: these people enjoyed the provisions of life for a long time; for this reason their hears hardened.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The reminder” means God's reminder about the Hereafter, so people would not forget it; the theme also appears in 21:44 and 28:45.
rows.anchor: refers to the reminder sounded to these people by God regarding the hereafter so that they do not forget it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word būr can describe singular or plural entities and can be masculine or feminine.
rows.anchor: is used for both singular and plural as well as masculine and feminine entities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For eloquence, the verse states a future event in the past tense.
rows.anchor: In deference to eloquence, a future event is mentioned in the past tense.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idolaters claim their deities commanded them to worship them, but the deities will deny associating anyone with God or commanding such worship.
rows.anchor: The Idolaters claimed that their deities had commanded them to worship them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After this conclusive denial, the idolaters have no defense; shirk merits great punishment because the Qur’an calls it great oppression.
rows.anchor: This is because polytheism is called

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though it appears to address the Prophet, the verse addresses the masses, explaining its use of both singular and plural verbs and pronouns.
rows.anchor: Though this verse apparently addresses the Prophet (sws), it is evident from its words that it is directed towards the masses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers the objection in 25:7: earlier messengers ate and walked in markets like ordinary people, so these activities do not undermine prophethood.
rows.anchor: The verse actually answers the objection cited in verse 7 earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs recognized Abraham and Ishmael as prophets and took pride in their descent and religion, while regarding them as human rather than superhuman.
rows.anchor: At the same time, the Arabs never claimed that these two were superhuman.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Israelites likewise did not consider their prophets superhuman; the Qur’an elsewhere tells objectors to consult the People of the Book about prophetic history.
rows.anchor: they should consult the People of the Book – who are well aware of this history – whether these prophets ate food and roamed the markets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Christians since Paul tried to make Jesus superhuman, the Gospels attest that Jesus and Mary ate; the Qur’an uses this in 5:75 as evidence against their divinity.
rows.anchor: In verse 75 of S ūrah al-Mā’idah, the words used are M (both of them ate food).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers’ poverty tests disbelievers who object that revelation should have gone to wealthy people of Makkah or Ṭā’if; God’s favour instead fuels their arrogance and mockery. This parallels 6:53.
rows.anchor: In other words, the poverty of the Muslims has become a trial for the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Would you show patience?” is addressed to believers: disbelievers have failed their test of gratitude, and believers should persevere through mockery and enmity.
rows.anchor: The words “would you show patience?” are addressed to the believers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exhortation is phrased as information, and an interrogative further intensifies it; the author points to 26:39 for explanation.
rows.anchor: If a letter of interrogation is added, it further increases this emphasis.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those who do not fear coming before Us” describes arrogant people whose conceit exceeds that of other active opponents; it exposes arrogance rather than merely naming disbelief.
rows.anchor: those arrogant people who did not have any fear of appearing before God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They demand that angels come to them or that God reveal Himself directly, a demand so arrogant and foolish that the Qur’an attacks their conceit instead of answering it.
rows.anchor: This group demanded that if an angel comes to Muḥammad (sws) as he claimed, then why do not angels come to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One meaning of ḥijran maḥjūrā is a strong barrier or divide, as in 25:53.
rows.anchor: a strong barrier and divide.” In verse 53 of this sūrah, this expression occurs in this meaning.

rows.speaker: S ībawayah
rows.claim: A second meaning is seeking refuge; Sībawayah says the phrase is used in this exact form, with its accusative governed by an elided verb, as in “maʿādh Allāh.”
rows.anchor: the opinion of S ībawayah (d. 180 AH), when it occurs in this meaning, it is used in precisely this way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims should leave opponents to their fate and courageously endure their own trial of patience.
rows.anchor: consign them to their fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God watches over the Prophet and will help him reach his destination through opposition if he perseveres.
rows.anchor: If he shows perseverance, the Almighty will make him reach his destination in spite of all this opposition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God describes the trial as His own act and says this subject has been explained at several other points in the exegesis.
rows.anchor: God had ascribed the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their deeds seemed to secure high status in worldly life, but the verse says God will render them dust.
rows.anchor: status because of them. The verse says that all these deeds will be scattered like dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will turn their deeds to dust because deeds not done purely for Him have no value before Him.
rows.anchor: because deeds not done to purely please Him have no value before Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about God moving toward each deed indicates that He takes the initiative to reject all their deeds, large or small, humiliating them.
rows.anchor: shows that God will take the initiative to reject their deeds, whether big or small.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This scene contrasts with the People of Paradise, whom disbelievers had looked down on in worldly life.
rows.anchor: This is in contrast is the portrayal of the People of Paradise, which the disbelievers looked down upon in the previous world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imru’ al-Qays’s couplet witnesses maqīl as a place of relaxation or rest.
rows.anchor: relax in a relaxing place that is secure from every bad omen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maqīl literally means a place for siesta and more generally a resting or relaxing place.
rows.anchor: In its general usage, it refers to a resting place and a relaxing space.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥsan and maqīlan are not comparative forms here; they mean something best and grand without comparison.
rows.anchor: are not meant for comparison here. They refer to something best and grand without any comparison.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Biting the hand conveys regret and longing, an expression also found in other languages.
rows.anchor: Biting the hand signifies regret and longing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Unjust” refers to someone who is unjust to himself.
rows.anchor: The word “unjust” here refers to someone who is unjust to his own self.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sovereignty statement continues the answer to those who earlier demanded to see angels.
rows.anchor: These words are part of the answer given earlier to those who were demanding to see angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has always held true authority, but its veil in this world lets fools imagine they are sovereign; Judgment Day will show that all authority belongs to God alone.
rows.anchor: On the Day of Judgement, however, it will become evident to everyone that all power and authority rests with God and none else.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Unjust” refers to a person who wrongs himself; this covers anyone who opposed the messenger.
rows.anchor: it alludes to every person who opposed the messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ʿan after ḍalla adds the sense of turning away; false statements against the Messenger and God’s Book led the speaker away from the Messenger’s path.
rows.anchor: shows that the latter encompasses the meaning of withdrawal.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His admission that the reminder came to him concedes his own wretchedness: once truth was fully conveyed, he had no excuse.
rows.anchor: The expression “after it had come to me” is his confession of his own wretchedness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word khadhūl refers to someone insincere and treacherous.
rows.anchor: refers to someone who is insincere and is a traitor.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the common reading, the statement that Satan is unfaithful to humans is God’s immediate reminder, not part of the regretful person’s speech.
rows.anchor: is not part of the statement of those who were regretful, as has been generally understood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here Satan is generic, referring to devils among humans and jinn; leaders and followers who spread deviance together will curse and blame one another in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The word “Satan” here is a generic noun and refers to the devils found both among human beings and the jinn.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The messenger” is Muhammad, who will complain that his people ignored and rejected the Qur’an despite his earnest presentation; this complaint will be the final proof against them.
rows.anchor: The word “messenger” here refers to Muḥammad (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger says he presented the Book earnestly, but his people did not value it and rejected it.
rows.anchor: I presented this Book with full earnestness and sincerity before my people but they did not value it and totally rejected it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mā’idah discusses every messenger bearing witness about their people on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: every messenger will bear witness about their respective nations.
